claim: In brainstorming, people working alone and pooled afterwards (nominal groups) produced nearly twice as many different ideas as real interacting groups, contrary to Osborn's claim.
quote: Contrary to Osborn's claim, Taylor et al. found that nominal groups produced nearly twice as many different ideas as the real groups.
authors: Diehl, M.; Stroebe, W.
title: Productivity loss in brainstorming groups: Toward the solution of a riddle
venue: Journal of Personality and Social Psychology 53(3), 497-509
n: 4 experiments plus a table of 22 earlier experiments
transfer: Do not run agents as a talking group that sees each other's ideas. Generate ideas in independent calls, then pool and de-duplicate. Matches our NoveltyBench win.

claim: Of 22 earlier experiments, 18 found nominal groups better than real groups on idea count; only 4 (all two-person groups) found no difference.
quote: Of the 22 experiments listed in Table 1, 18 reported the performance of nominal groups to be superior to that of real groups, and only 4, all involving 2-person groups
authors: Diehl, M.; Stroebe, W.
title: Productivity loss in brainstorming groups: Toward the solution of a riddle
venue: Journal of Personality and Social Psychology 53(3), 497-509
transfer: Boundary: the group penalty was absent for 2-person groups. A two-agent pair is a weaker risk than a large panel, but independence is still the safe default.

claim: Direct manipulation showed production blocking (waiting for a turn) accounted for most of the productivity loss; evaluation apprehension was doubted as a major cause.
quote: by manipulating blocking directly, we determined in Experiment 4 that production blocking accounted for most of the productivity loss of real brainstorming groups.
authors: Diehl, M.; Stroebe, W.
title: Productivity loss in brainstorming groups: Toward the solution of a riddle
venue: Journal of Personality and Social Psychology 53(3), 497-509
transfer: Blocking has no direct LLM analogue (calls run in parallel). The lesson that survives: earlier ideas anchor later ones, so do not show earlier ideas to the generator.

claim: On idea quality, the earlier studies were mixed, but in all six that measured total quality, nominal groups did better than real groups.
quote: In all six studies that assessed total quality, nominal groups performed better than real groups did.
authors: Diehl, M.; Stroebe, W.
title: Productivity loss in brainstorming groups: Toward the solution of a riddle
venue: Journal of Personality and Social Psychology 53(3), 497-509
transfer: Total quality tracks idea count, so a quality gain from more ideas is partly a count effect. Our evaluator should score the best ideas, not the sum.

claim: Meta-analysis of brainstorming found nominal groups generally better than interacting groups, with the gap larger for bigger groups. Known to me only from a secondary summary.
quote: nominal groups are generally better than interacting brainstorming groups, with the gap larger when there are more people
authors: Mullen, B.; Johnson, C.; Salas, E.
title: Productivity loss in brainstorming groups: A meta-analytic integration
transfer: Adding more interacting agents to a debate should make idea output worse, not better. Keep generators independent.

claim: A meta-analysis found deliberate practice explains well under half of performance variance in every domain, and almost none in professions.
quote: games (26%), music (21%), sports (18%), education (4%), and professions (<1%).
authors: Macnamara, B. N.; Hambrick, D. Z.; Oswald, F. L. (as summarised by Macnamara, Moreau, Hambrick)
title: Deliberate practice and performance in music, games, sports, education, and professions: A meta-analysis
venue: Psychological Science 25(8); numbers read in Perspectives on Psychological Science 11(3), 2016
transfer: TRAIT/HISTORY, cannot transfer. Practice amount is a life history, not a thinking step. A model cannot be practised at run time. Only the fixed-model analogue (a lessons ledger) is a design choice, not evidence.

claim: Among elite sports performers, deliberate practice accounted for only about 1% of performance variance; overall it was 18%.
quote: deliberate practice accounted for only 1% of the variance in performance among elite-level performers.
authors: Macnamara, B. N.; Moreau, D.; Hambrick, D. Z.
title: The relationship between deliberate practice and performance in sports: A meta-analysis
n: 33 sport studies (count from a search summary; abstract does not state it)
transfer: TRAIT/HISTORY, cannot transfer. Range restriction at the top may explain the 1%. None for the agent.

claim: Athletes who reached high skill did not start their sport earlier in childhood than lower-skill athletes, which challenges the early-start claim.
quote: athletes who reached a high level of skill did not begin their sport earlier in childhood than lower skill athletes.
authors: Macnamara, B. N.; Moreau, D.; Hambrick, D. Z.
title: The relationship between deliberate practice and performance in sports: A meta-analysis
transfer: none (a developmental history fact, cannot transfer)

claim: Chess players varied enormously in practice needed to reach master level, from 3,016 to 23,608 hours.
quote: Gobet and Campitelli (2007) found a large amount of variability in the total amount of deliberate practice it took chess players to first reach "master" status--from 3,016 hr to 23,608 hr.
authors: Gobet, F.; Campitelli, G. (as cited by Macnamara et al.)
title: The role of domain-specific practice, handedness, and starting age in chess
venue: Developmental Psychology; read via Macnamara et al. 2016
transfer: none. Shows expertise is not a dose of hours. Gains per hour of chunking differ by person, a trait we cannot copy.

claim: The deliberate-practice numbers were disputed on statistics too: a critique argued a music correlation of 0.61 should not be read as 36% of variance, while the original authors reported about a third of reliable variance in chess and music.
quote: about one-third of the reliable variance in performance
authors: Hambrick, D. Z.; Oswald, F. L.; Altmann, E. M.; Meinz, E. J.; Gobet, F.; Campitelli, G. (reply to Platz et al.)
title: Facing facts about deliberate practice
transfer: Headline numbers depend on how variance is read. Do not import a practice-hours number into the design.

claim: The original deliberate-practice claim rested on retrospective estimates from groups of musicians, and the 10,000 hours figure was a group average for the best violinists, not a threshold.
quote: on average, the "best" violinists had accumulated over 10,000 hr of deliberate practice, compared with less than 8,000 hr for the "good" violinists
authors: Ericsson, K. A.; Krampe, R.; Tesch-Romer, C. (as described by Macnamara et al.)
title: The role of deliberate practice in the acquisition of expert performance
venue: Psychological Review; read via Macnamara et al. 2016
n: two studies of musicians (per Macnamara et al.)
transfer: none. Retrospective self-report and a popular rule built on one average. Treat practice-makes-expert as a story, not a step.

claim: Incubation (setting a problem aside) has a positive average effect on problem solving, but earlier studies conflicted, and the effect is larger for divergent thinking than for insight puzzles.
quote: The authors identified a positive incubation effect, with divergent thinking tasks benefiting more than linguistic and visual insight tasks from incubation.
authors: Sio, U. N.; Ormerod, T. C.
title: Does incubation enhance problem solving? A meta-analytic review
n: not read in the opened text (a secondary source says 117 studies, mean d about 0.29, unverified)
transfer: A pause step makes sense for open divergent tasks only. For a model, a break is just a new call with a fresh sample; the human memory-decay mechanism does not transfer, only the effect shape.

claim: Incubation was weaker when the break was filled with a demanding task, and for word insight problems an easy task beat plain rest. Conditions matter.
quote: filling an incubation period with high cognitive demand tasks gave a smaller incubation effect. Surprisingly, low cognitive demand tasks yielded a stronger incubation effect than did rest
authors: Sio, U. N.; Ormerod, T. C.
title: Does incubation enhance problem solving? A meta-analytic review
transfer: Do not add a generic incubate step. If used, gate it to open tasks after a real impasse, and keep the interpolated work light.

claim: Before the meta-analysis, incubation studies disagreed: some found strong effects, others none, and some researchers doubted the effect existed.
quote: some studies reporting strong effects (e.g., Smith & Blankenship, 1989) and others failing to find any effect at all (Olton & Johnson, 1976)
authors: Sio, U. N.; Ormerod, T. C.
title: Does incubation enhance problem solving? A meta-analytic review
transfer: Incubation is a fragile effect. Test it in our harness against a no-break control before keeping it.

claim: In chess Einstellung, experts did not beat novices when the familiar move was merely suboptimal: 8 of 17 experts and 8 of 17 novices chose it and kept looking at it.
quote: Equal numbers of experts and novices (8 of 17 each) chose it.
authors: Sheridan, H.; Reingold, E. M.
title: The mechanisms and boundary conditions of the Einstellung effect in chess: Evidence from eye movements
transfer: Expertise does not protect against a good-enough familiar answer. When the first answer works but is not best, nothing triggers search. Ask for a rival only when a check says it could be better. Fits our rule: trust the first answer until a check fails. (Quote is from the fetch tool's paraphrase of the paper, not confirmed word for word.)

claim: When the familiar move was a clear blunder, almost everyone avoided it. A failure signal, not a schedule, drives the switch.
quote: All of the experts and the majority of the novices were able to avoid selecting the Einstellung move.
authors: Sheridan, H.; Reingold, E. M.
title: The mechanisms and boundary conditions of the Einstellung effect in chess: Evidence from eye movements
transfer: Supports impasse-triggered doubt: run a real check, and only a failed check opens the search for alternatives.

claim: Experts first fixated the target region faster than novices (407 ms vs 719 ms), with shorter, more frequent looks. This is a fast perceptual pattern skill.
quote: Experts first fixated the target region faster (407 ms vs. 719 ms)
authors: Sheridan, H.; Reingold, E. M.
title: The mechanisms and boundary conditions of the Einstellung effect in chess: Evidence from eye movements
transfer: TRAIT/PERCEPTION, cannot transfer (human eye movements). Chunk-based fast recognition is already in the model's weights.

claim: For LLMs, revising an answer with no outside feedback does not help reasoning and can make it worse.
quote: LLMs struggle to self-correct their responses without external feedback, and at times their performance even degrades after self-correction.
authors: Huang, J.; Chen, X.; Mishra, S.; et al.
title: Large Language Models Cannot Self-Correct Reasoning Yet
transfer: A human-style reconsider-your-answer step is a case where the recommended method made models worse. Every doubt step needs an external signal (test, run, tool), as in plan principle 3.

claim: Jansson and Smith's design fixation study is the standard demonstration that shown examples lead designers to copy example features. I did not open it; known from secondary pages.
quote: Jansson and Smith [16] were the first to demonstrate fixation experimentally in engineering design.
authors: Jansson, D. G.; Smith, S. M.
title: Design fixation
transfer: Showing the model earlier candidate ideas anchors it. Generate before showing any example or prior answer; show examples only as things to differ from.

claim: A critical review contrasts two accounts of example effects: unconscious conformity, or examples simply using up the pool of likely solutions before search starts. This is a boundary on the fixation story.
quote: unconscious conformity or a product of sampling probability
authors: unknown (Design Society paper, not read)
title: Exposure effects in design idea generation: unconscious conformity or a product of sampling probability
transfer: If it is sampling probability, a model fixes on common answers by default, and the fix is explicit exclusion of earlier answers, not a mindset change. Year and authors unknown; re-check before relying.

claim: Telling design teams about fixation reduced fixation elements in their work in one study using the Jansson and Smith problems.
quote: educating each team on the phenomena and effects of design fixation reduced the number of fixation elements in comparison to the control group
authors: unknown (ICED 2013 paper, via search snippet)
title: Overcoming design fixation through education and creativity methods
transfer: Weak hint that naming the trap in the prompt can help. Untested for models, and our own results show forced doubt can hurt. Test only on open tasks.

claim: Writing ideas down while waiting for a turn did not remove the group brainstorming penalty. A simple patch to a bad procedure did not rescue it.
quote: research has shown that it does not increase the quantity of ideas produced
authors: Diehl, M.; Stroebe, W. (1991), as cited by an encyclopedia page
title: Production blocking (encyclopedia summary)
transfer: Low weight: secondary source. Prefer redesign (independence) to patching.

claim: Large electronic brainstorming groups (no turn-taking) are reported to beat nominal groups in a meta-analysis, so the group penalty is removable under some conditions. Known only from a search summary.
quote: large electronic brainstorming groups generated more and better ideas than nominal brainstorming groups
authors: Derosa, D. M.; Smith, C. L.; Hantula, D. A.
title: Electronic group brainstorming meta-analysis (exact title not verified)
transfer: Boundary: the penalty depends on blocking. LLM calls run in parallel, but they share anchoring. URL is generic because I did not open the paper; find the real one before citing. Quote is the summarizer's wording.

claim: Within a domain, experts resisted mental-set rigidity more than novices in one management and grammar study. This contrasts with the chess result where expertise did not help on a suboptimal familiar move.
quote: experts resisted mental-set rigidity within their own domain more than novices did
authors: unknown (Jagiellonian University repository, via search snippet)
title: How non-experts fail where experts do not: implications of expertise for resistance to cognitive rigidity
transfer: Mixed evidence on whether expertise protects against set. Do not assume a strong model resists its own default answers. The quote is the summarizer's wording, not the source's.
